title: Identity, Directory Sync and Audit Export in the Open-Source Rendezvous
description: OIDC/JWT validation, identity bridges, directory sync, blueprint provisioning and Splunk, CEF or JSON audit export in the Pilot rendezvous you run yourself.
seoTitle: Identity, Directory Sync and Audit Export | Pilot Protocol
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: This post was first published in March 2026 as an implementation milestone. It now describes the open-source rendezvous at

v1.18.0. Every command here needs the registry's admin token. On the public backbone that token is held by its operators, so these features are for a registry you run yourself. There is no managed or hosted version.

Beyond roles and policies, the Pilot rendezvous can validate OIDC tokens, bind nodes to identities from your directory, sync directory membership into network roles, provision a whole network from one JSON blueprint, and export its audit trail to Splunk, a CEF collector or any JSON endpoint. This post walks through each, with the commands and messages that drive them.

The registry checks the flag in the handlers for promote, demote, kick, transfer ownership, set policy, invite, respond to invite, set key expiry and directory sync. Against a network without the flag each returns an error that starts with
The registry stores one identity-provider configuration for the whole registry. Its type is one of

, but the check the registry performs itself is the same for all of them: it validates a JWT against the configured JWKS URL. Providers that issue OIDC tokens (Entra ID and most cloud identity services) work through that path. SAML, LDAP and anything else need a bridge you run, described below.

fields.code:
# Configure an OIDC provider
pilotctl extras idp set --type oidc \
  --url https://login.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json \
  --issuer https://login.example.com/ \
  --client-id pilot-prod

# Show the current configuration
pilotctl extras idp get

children.text: registry message checks a token directly, with no sidecar or proxy. Two algorithms are supported:
- RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256, with keys from the provider's JWKS endpoint.
- HMAC-SHA256 with a symmetric key from the JWKS document.
against the client ID (string or array),

, with 60 seconds of clock skew allowed. The registry also requires the JWKS key type and algorithm to match the token header, so an HS256 token can't be verified with an RSA public key used as an HMAC secret.
JWKS keys are cached for 5 minutes, keyed by URL and
. A non-200 response from the JWKS endpoint is an error, and the response body is capped at 64 KB.

Either way, the identity check happens in code you control. The registry does not speak SAML or LDAP itself.
A directory export (from Active Directory, Entra ID, LDAP or anything else you can script) is pushed to the registry as a list of entries. The registry maps entries to nodes by
An entry with a role (owner, admin or member) sets that node's role in the network.

An entry with no matching node yet becomes a role pre-assignment, applied when a node with that external ID joins.

The command prints how many entries were mapped, updated, disabled and left unmapped, followed by one line per change. Directory sync requires the enterprise flag on the network.
A blueprint declares a network's configuration in one JSON document. The
) creates the network or finds it by name, sets the enterprise flag, applies the policy, configures the identity provider, sets webhooks and audit export, and stores role pre-assignments.

fields.code:
# prod-fleet.json
{
  "name": "prod-fleet",
  "join_rule": "invite",
  "enterprise": true,
  "policy": {
    "max_members": 100,
    "allowed_ports": [7, 80, 443, 1001],
    "description": "Production agent fleet"
  },
  "identity_provider": {
    "type": "oidc",
    "url": "https://login.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    "issuer": "https://login.example.com/",
    "client_id": "pilot-prod"
  },
  "webhooks": {
    "audit_url": "https://siem.example.com/pilot/events"
  },
  "audit_export": {
    "format": "splunk_hec",
    "endpoint": "https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector",
    "token": "HEC-TOKEN",
    "index": "pilot_audit",
    "source": "pilot-registry"
  },
  "roles": [
    {"external_id": "alice@example.com", "role": "owner"},
    {"external_id": "bob@example.com", "role": "admin"},
    {"external_id": "charlie@example.com", "role": "member"}
  ]
}

# Apply it
pilotctl extras provision prod-fleet.json
provisioned network 3 (prod-fleet)
  - created network 3 (prod-fleet)
  - enabled enterprise features
  - applied network policy
  - configured oidc identity provider
  - configured audit webhook
  - configured splunk_hec audit export to https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector
  - stored 3 RBAC pre-assignments

children.text: The blueprint is validated before anything changes: unknown join rules, a token-gated network without
, unknown roles or identity-provider types, unknown audit export formats and unsafe URLs are rejected. Running the same blueprint again finds the network by name and reapplies the settings.

Audit events go to the structured log, the registry webhook and, when configured, the audit exporter. The exporter posts each event over HTTP in one of three formats:
An HTTP Event Collector payload with
object. The token is sent as
One Common Event Format line per event, posted as

. Severity is 6 for kick and delete actions, 4 for promote and demote, and 3 for everything else. Extensions carry the action, network ID and node ID, and user-controlled fields are escaped so they can't inject extra fields.

fields.code:
# Send audit events to Splunk
pilotctl extras audit-export set --format splunk_hec \
  --endpoint https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector \
  --splunk-token HEC-TOKEN --index pilot_audit

# Show the configuration and exported/dropped counts
pilotctl extras audit-export get

# Turn it off
pilotctl extras audit-export disable

children.text: The exporter runs in the background with a 1,024-event buffer. Each event gets up to three attempts on network errors and 5xx responses, waiting 1 s and then 2 s. If the buffer is full, events are dropped and counted rather than blocking the registry.
Registry Webhook and Dead Letter Queue
The registry has its own webhook, set with

, separate from each daemon's. It retries the same way as the exporter. A 4xx response goes straight to a dead letter queue without retry, and so does an event that fails every attempt. The queue keeps the last 100 failed events for inspection with
. With a secret configured on the registry, each body is signed with HMAC-SHA256 in
, and webhook URLs must be http or https and cannot point at link-local addresses or cloud metadata endpoints.
